what_it_does: Processors spend a lot of time waiting for data to arrive from main memory (the large but slow chip that stores the program's data). Prefetching — guessing which memory locations will be needed soon and loading them into the processor's fast on-chip cache before they are requested — can hide that wait time. For programs that chase pointers or walk irregular data structures, the access pattern is hard to predict geometrically, but there is often a temporal pattern: the same sequence of addresses tends to appear together whenever a particular code path runs. Hardware temporal prefetchers record recent access sequences in a metadata table and replay them when they see the start of a known sequence, but the table has limited capacity and prior software-guided techniques for managing what to keep in it barely improved over no guidance at all. Prophet is a hardware-software co-design that profiles a program's memory behavior using lightweight hardware event counters, then uses a compiler step to insert small hints directly into the program binary. At runtime, these hints tell the hardware prefetcher which sequence-tracking entries are most worth preserving for frequently executed code paths, letting the prefetcher concentrate its limited table space where it will provide the biggest benefit, while falling back to unguided behavior for less frequent paths.
